query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dominant mechanism governing the improved wear performance of high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is the shear-induced formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer via dynamic amorphization. This layer, generated under sliding wear, significantly reduces friction by enabling grain boundary sliding and suppressing dislocation-driven mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a baseline nanocrystalline or partially amorphous microstructure produced under standard processing (baseline deposition temperature/sputtering power), exhibiting limited pre-existing dynamic amorphization.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the deposition temperature (or sputtering power) during coating fabrication to promote or suppress the material’s propensity for dynamic amorphization. This controlled processing change is intended to modulate the extent to which an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer forms during subsequent wear.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted under sliding conditions in an inert (or ultra-high vacuum) environment to minimize oxidation, with moderate-to-high loads and speeds that are known to induce shear-related microstructural evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of dynamic amorphization resulting in the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer.
generation.mechanism: Increased deposition temperature (or sputtering power) enhances the free energy stored in the coating, making it more susceptible to shear-induced dynamic amorphization during wear. The resulting ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior, lowering the shear strength at the interface and thereby reducing friction and wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings processed under conditions that favor dynamic amorphization are expected to generate a thicker and more continuous ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer during wear, leading to lower friction coefficients (e.g., closer to 0.2–0.3) and reduced wear rates compared to baseline coatings processed at lower deposition temperatures or power settings.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings produced under standard processing conditions that generate a microstructure with less predisposition to dynamic amorphization, which show higher friction coefficients and wear rates under identical wear conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for HEA coatings with compositions similar to CoCrFeMnNi and under wear testing regimes that promote high strain rate shear (moderate-to-high load and velocity) in inert or controlled atmospheres. It may not directly apply in high-temperature or oxidizing environments where additional tribochemical effects can dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in friction and wear rate attributable solely to dynamic amorphization is uncertain due to potential overlapping contributions from static properties such as hardness and phase coexistence. Additionally, the sensitivity of dynamic amorphization to slight variations in processing conditions needs further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) coatings: one produced under the baseline deposition conditions and one under modified deposition conditions (e.g., elevated temperature or increased sputtering power) designed to promote dynamic amorphization. Subject both groups to identical sliding wear tests under inert conditions while periodically characterizing the worn surfaces via TEM or STEM to assess the presence and thickness of the ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer.
measurements: Friction coefficient via tribometer during sliding wear
Wear rate determination (e.g., mass loss or profilometry)
Microstructural analysis (TEM/STEM) to quantify the formation and extent of the dynamic amorphized surface layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coatings processed under the conditions intended to promote dynamic amorphization do not develop a significantly thicker or more continuous ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous layer, or if they do not exhibit consistently lower friction coefficients and wear rates compared to the baseline group, then the hypothesis that dynamic amorphization is the dominant mechanism governing improved wear performance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have inspired considerable interest due to their attractive physical and mechanical properties. In this work, the microstructural evolution induced by different heat treatments on rapidly solidified hypoeutectic precursors of a Fe26.7Co26.7Ni26.7Si8.9B11 HEA is investigated and correlated with the corresponding mechanical properties. The microstructures of the rapidly solidified precursors are composed of primary fcc solid solution dendrites embedded in a eutectic matrix. When the samples are annealed at different temperatures after furnace cooling or quenching, respectively, the eutectic structure gradually decomposes into fcc, tetragonal (Fe,Co)2B, and hexagonal Ni31Si12 crystals with increasing annealing temperature, leading to a gradual increase of the content of the fcc crystals and both their aggregation and coarsening. Then the dominant structural framework gradually transforms from eutectic structures to fcc dendrites and ultimately the (Fe,Co)2B crystals become isolated as dominant reinforcement particles distributed in the interdendritic regions. AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. Recent work has shown that low friction of bare metals, in the range μ≅0.2−0.5, can be explained as the dynamic softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) of surfaces due to highly surface-localized, shear-induced severe plastic deformation,,. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties and physically meaningful input parameters like temperature and shear rate. frame.system: High-entropy-alloy (HEA) protective coatings designed for wear-resistant applications, typically processed to yield a baseline microstructure (e.g., nanocrystalline or partially amorphous with high compositional disorder and multiple principal elements).
frame.goal: To isolate and verify the primary mechanistic factor governing the wear performance of HEA coatings, thereby explaining why adjustments in composition, phase distribution, or microstructural features enhance resistance to wear.
frame.limitation: A lack of a single, unified mechanistic explanation that links the unique multi-principal element composition and resulting microstructure with the observed wear performance, making it unclear which feature (e.g., high hardness, phase transformation under stress, or grain boundary sliding) is dominant.

decision.trend: Early studies initially correlated properties such as hardness and phase composition with improved wear performance in HEAs. Subsequent work showed that wear tests are accompanied by dynamic evolution of the microstructure – for example, the formation of ultrafine (ultra‐nanocrystalline) or amorphous surface layers (dynamic amorphization) and adaptive oxide nanocomposites – that in turn lower friction and wear rates. The progression has been from empirical “hardness equals low wear” observations toward proposing that a controlled microstructural transition under sliding (e.g., grain refinement or reactive nanolayer formation) is critical. However, even with these insights, the dominant mechanistic “lever” has not been isolated.
decision.unsolved: A single, testable mechanistic hypothesis linking the unique multi‐principal element, often nanocrystalline or partially amorphous, microstructure of HEA protective coatings to their excellent wear resistance remains unconfirmed. In particular, it is unclear whether the dynamic evolution (e.g., the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer during wear) is the central mechanism, or if static microstructural factors like hardness or phase coexistence play a greater role.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the processing parameters—such as deposition temperature or sputtering power—to modulate the degree of dynamic amorphization (and hence the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer) while keeping the overall alloy composition fixed.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend seen in earlier studies where microstructure evolution during wear (e.g., grain refinement or adaptive layer formation) correlated with improved performance. By isolating and controlling the formation of a dynamically induced nano/amorphous layer, the experiment can test whether this microstructural transition is the dominant mechanism governing wear resistance over the baseline microstructure.
